 Which small businesses need cyber liability insurance most?
 By Stacker 
 Published 
 October 29, 2026 
 2:43 pm 
 By Mary Beth Eastman for ERGO NEXT
 Data from the nonprofit Identity Theft Resource Center’s 2025 Business Impact Report found that 81% of small businesses surveyed reported a security breach , a data breach, or both in the last year. Cyber liability insurance could help protect small businesses from some of the costs of data breaches, ransomware or hacking.
 E-commerce retailers or digital service providers who run their business online are clearly exposed to risk. But so are professional service providers, such as accountants and other financial services firms, consultants, creatives like graphic designers or writers, and real estate professionals like agents or brokers.
 If your work involves electronic information and communications, keep reading. ERGO NEXT  shares ways to help protect yourself and your business from the rising threats of digital vulnerability and the costs associated with an attack.
 Twenty-seven percent of small business owners rank a cyberattack or data breach among their top concerns, according to an ERGO NEXT 2026 survey  of 501 small business owners. And about a third of those surveyed — 31% — said it was the risk they felt least prepared to handle. And the Identity Theft Resource Center  found that 63% of breached small businesses suffered losses of $250,000 or more, causing many to raise prices to cover the cost.
 Some small business owners think they’re too small to attract the attention of cybercriminals. But their small size is precisely what makes them an attractive target, says Shawn Silver, founder and CEO of payment processing company Payment Nerds . He has a front-row seat to the risks small businesses regularly face from hackers.    
 “ Cybercriminals  aren’t looking for the biggest company,” he says. “They’re looking for a way in, and a small business can be perfect.” A compromised login could open the door for a hacker to gain unauthorized access to client data and financial information, putting a business at serious risk.
 Which industries could benefit from cyber liability insurance most?
 The businesses most likely to face cyber risk  are those in high-risk industries, such as financial services.  “Any company that processes digital payments or handles customer data has exposure,” Silver says.
 These industries can include:
 Accountants 
 Consultants 
 Software developers 
 Insurance professionals 
 Retailers , including e-commerce  
 Restaurant  owners
 Real estate professionals 
 Your business might benefit from cyber liability insurance  if you:
 Collect sensitive client information such as birth dates, Social Security numbers or bank account information
 Accept credit card payments or use a POS system
 Send and receive invoices and payments by email or wire
 Regularly log in to client systems or accounts
 Rely on cloud software or email for daily operations
 Are required by clients or contracts to carry this type of business insurance coverage
 “We tend to see businesses across e-commerce, subscription models, healthcare and telemedicine, professional services, and other large-scale digital transactions as highly targeted,” Silver reports.
 ERGO NEXT 
 Top cyber threats by industry
 The cyber risks a business might face depend on size, industry, and many other factors. But as technology evolves, so do black-hat tactics.
 “Small businesses are starting to deal with the consequences of phishing and stolen credentials, account takeover, ransomware, payment fraud, and compromised customer data,” Silver says.
 Here’s what those risks can look like in real life.
 1.Consultants: Costly client data exposure 
 Consultants trade and rely on information to provide results for their clients. Email inboxes and shared drives can hold a trove of valuable data, such as strategy documents and client financials. This turns your email account into a valuable key that can unlock data for cybercriminals.
 Business email compromise (BEC) is when a criminal hacks an email account to access data or redirect funds. BEC caused about $3 billion in reported losses in 2025, according to the FBI’s Internet Crime Report .
 Many consultants carry professional liability insurance , also called errors and omissions (E&O) insurance , to help protect against claims that their professional errors or mistakes cost their client money. But data breaches are a different kind of risk. Consultants can add cyber liability insurance to their professional liability policy to help cover costs that arise from a breach.
 2. Financial professionals: Hacked financial data 
 Accountants, bookkeepers, brokers, advisors and tax professionals have access to extremely valuable data: Personal identity and financial information.
 As a financial professional, documents containing client data such as SSNs, IRS identifiers or bank account numbers regularly pass through your inbox. A breach at your business could lead to client notification costs, credit monitoring services or regulatory penalties. Cyber liability insurance could help cover those expenses after a covered event.
 3. Real estate agents: Wire fraud for large sums 
 As a real estate agent or broker, you regularly transact deals involving steep amounts of money, often transferred from one party to another via wire. Contracts often have tight deadlines and rapid turnarounds, with many different parties on an email thread.
 Criminals know this, too. Which is why they often target real estate firms and title companies. It’s not uncommon for them to spoof an email and divert funds using fraudulent wiring instructions.
 The FBI received more than 12,000 complaints  of real estate fraud in 2025, with more than $275 million in reported losses.
 4. Creative services: Compromised client accounts 
 Marketing agencies, designers, IT consultants and software developers, copywriters and other professionals often hold sensitive client login information. Cybercriminals target creatives and agencies through phishing, social engineering and other tactics to try to gain access to this information — which is exactly what happened to Tricia Mirchandani, founder of the marketing firm T Collective , based in Virginia.
 A prospective “client” made contact and invited her to a Zoom meeting to discuss potential marketing work.
 “[It] didn’t look right, but I clicked anyway,” she says. A teammate she had invited to the meeting also clicked. But instead of connecting her to a Zoom meeting, the link attempted to download malware to her computer, likely part of a scheme  to access clients’ sensitive business data.
 “Fortunately, the scam only worked on PCs, and we both have Macs, so no long-term damage was done,” Mirchandani says. Now the team has a firm rule: “We now never click until we fully verify where the link is coming from,” Mirchandani says.
 5. Retailers and restaurants: POS malware 
 For many small business owners who sell direct to customers, most or all of their revenue runs through a POS system. Cybercriminals install malware onto a POS to steal customer credit card data, or ransomware to lock the system a business needs to operate.
 Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report  found that ransomware appeared in 48% of all breaches it analyzed — up from 44% the previous year.
 “Any downtime or loss of a payment channel for a small business can create immediate cash flow issues,” Silver says.
 4 ways small businesses can fight back against cybercriminals
 You don’t need an IT department to increase cybersecurity at your business.
 1. Use secure payment hardware and software. Store as little payment data as possible and follow PCI standards, which are security rules set by the payment card industry.
 2. Lock down your logins with multi-factor authentication (MFA). MFA requires a second step, such as a code sent to your phone, every time you log in to your account. Zackery Nienaber, owner of Ohio-based Nienaber and Sons Lawn Care , added MFA to his accounts when he noticed numerous phishing attempts and suspicious login alerts on his business accounts. “Dealing with suspicious login attempts and spoofed messages aimed at our client data made us realize how quickly a localized operation can be disrupted if your digital defenses aren’t locked down,” he says.
 3. Verify before you pay (or click):  Confirm payments such as large wire transfers with a phone call to a number you already have, not one listed in an email. Do the same legwork for any unexpected links or “urgent” requests, even if they look fine at first.
 4. Train your team:  Sometimes all it takes is one careless moment to bring down your whole company. “Businesses can have the best tools in the world, but if an employee is tricked into giving up their access, the entire system is compromised,” Silver says. Provide regular team hacker training and refreshers on the latest scams so everyone knows how to spot red flags.
 “Cybersecurity should be thought of as a business function, not a one-time project,” Silver says. “Employees and vendors come and go, software is updated and your revenue streams evolve.” Your security practices should evolve, too.
 He recommends regularly reviewing answers to these three questions:
 Who has access to my systems?
 What sensitive data do I store?
 What happens to my business if my payment systems are shut off?
 “Small businesses dedicate a lot of time and energy to generating revenue,” he says. “They need to dedicate the same level of investment to protecting that revenue stream.”
 What Cyber Liability insurance could cover
 One of the best ways to protect your revenue stream against the cost of a cyberattack is with cyber liability insurance. Depending on your policy, this type of small business insurance  could help cover costs such as:
 Restoring your data after a ransomware attack
 Legal costs or regulatory penalties associated with a data breach
 Lost business income
 For example, if a criminal hacks the email inbox of your management consulting business, they might be able to access a client’s login credentials (and their personal data). Cyber liability insurance could help cover the cost of an investigation and your legal defense after a covered breach.
